Guardrails: Julian NOT used (post-Constantine trap); no claim that growth proves truth - the reel attributes the conduct to what the Christians believed.
voiceover: Around the year thirty, a Galilean teacher was executed on a Roman cross — and his movement should have died with him. No army. No wealth. At most a few hundred followers, in one corner of an empire. Three centuries later the emperor himself was a Christian — but by then the faith had already grown into the millions, while it was still illegal. Around the year 112 the Roman governor Pliny reported that it had spread through the cities, the villages and the countryside, among people of every age and rank. When plague struck Alexandria, its bishop wrote that Christians stayed with the dying and nursed them — many perishing as a result — while frightened neighbours abandoned their own. And they took in the children a whole civilisation discarded. By the year 251, one illegal congregation in Rome was supporting more than fifteen hundred widows and people in distress. Why live like that? Because they believed Jesus had been raised — and would one day ask what they had done. A tiny, powerless, illegal movement outlasted the empire that tried to kill it — not by force, which it never had, but by love, which it could not stop giving away.
